intro: The fourth of Webern’s Six Pieces for Orchestra, Op. 6, is a funeral march marked Langsam. It opens with bass drum, tam-tam and low bells, the strings are silent throughout, and Robert Craft conducts its gradual crescendo from a very soft start to a final loud passage for the percussion.

cues.title: Opening percussion, bars 1–10
cues.text: A bass-drum roll sounds under quiet strokes of tam-tam and low bells, which Webern places at a distance. The winds then enter. The strings do not play in this movement.
cues.evidence: Webern, Six Pieces, Op. 6, original 1909 version, Universal Edition, plate UE 6646, movement IV, bars 1–10, p. 16: bass drum, tam-tam and low bells placed at a distance, then winds; no strings appear in the movement. https://imslp.eu/files/imglnks/euimg/2/2d/IMSLP424298-PMLP02079-Op._6_6_Pieces_Original_copy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bass-drum strokes, bars 19–27
cues.text: An alto-flute phrase passes to horn and muted trumpet, over soft chords in muted trombones and tuba. The bass drum stops its continuous roll and plays separate strokes beneath the melody.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition, plate UE 6646, original 1909 version, movement IV, bars 19–27, pp. 17–18: alto flute, horn and muted-trumpet phrases over muted trombones and tuba; the bass drum has separate strokes from bar 19. https://imslp.eu/files/imglnks/euimg/2/2d/IMSLP424298-PMLP02079-Op._6_6_Pieces_Original_copy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brass climax and percussion crescendo
cues.text: Horns and trombones play their short phrases louder. The tempo then broadens as drums, tam-tam and bells grow beneath them. The wind instruments stop before the end, and the percussion plays the final crescendo alone.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition, plate UE 6646, original 1909 version, movement IV, bars 34–40, pp. 20–22: the brass climax, ritardando at rehearsal 10 and final percussion crescendo after the winds stop. https://imslp.eu/files/imglnks/euimg/2/2d/IMSLP424298-PMLP02079-Op._6_6_Pieces_Original_copy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The original labels and contemporary review name the orchestra and conductor. The fourth piece uses wind instruments and percussion; individual players are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: High Fidelity, September 1979, p. 129 explicitly identifies Craft's Columbia MS 6216 as the first version, distinguishing it from the 1928 revision in his separate complete-Webern set. The original score heads movement IV Langsam, marcia funebre; its central solo begins on alto flute, not the revision's clarinet. Section landmarks are broad score-proportion timings, without aural review.

fields.note: The label lists Schoenberg as band 1 and Webern's six pieces as bands 2–7; No. 4 is therefore band 5. The matrix is printed on the label. No session take or stamper suffix is asserted.

composer.background:
When Peter Stadlen prepared the first performance of Webern’s Piano Variations in Vienna in 1937, the composer covered his score with instructions about expression. One phrase needed more vigour; another was an echo. Webern compared the opening movement to a late Brahms intermezzo. In the preface to his annotated edition, published in 1979, Stadlen recalled a “fervently lyrical mind bent on expressiveness”.

Webern was born in Vienna on 3 December 1883 and grew up in Graz and Klagenfurt, with holidays at Preglhof, the family estate in Carinthia. His mother, Amalie, played the piano and sang; he learnt piano and cello and joined the orchestra of the local concert society. The family played chamber music together. Later, when he was living away from home, he wrote in his letters about the woods and meadows around Preglhof and about his mother’s grave at nearby Schwabegg.
